name: PT Sumber Alfaria Trijaya Tbk

frontmatter.title: Alfamart: a growth franchise priced for a store cap that does not yet exist
frontmatter.summary: The shares halved on a ministerial threat to stop new minimarket permits and an index exit, while stores, revenue and cash flow kept growing. A ten-year DCF at a house-band cost of capital says the market is paying for a permanent stall. BUY.
thesis: Expansion has not stopped: 1,081 net new Alfamart stores in 2025 and a 800 target for 2026, against a ministerial statement about new permits only and one regency enforcing a rule in force since 2021.
Last-actual economics are stable: gross margin held at 21.9% through FY2025 and the first nine months of FY2026, operating margin 3.6% on the restated basis.
The de-rating did the damage, not the earnings: 12.7x forward earnings and 4.2x EV/EBITDA against a five-year average in the high twenties.
Net cash, negative working capital and a 50.0% payout support a 3.9% yield while the growth is re-priced.
Base case Rp1,351 a share, probability-weighted target Rp1,531; the bear case values the equity at Rp506, roughly half today's price, and is the honest downside.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results: fourth-quarter revenue and the full-year net operating-expense ratio
FY2027 expansion plan published with the annual report
Annual general meeting: FY2026 final dividend and payout policy
Vietnam entry: first stores if the local partner is signed

blocks.text: **BUY. Target Rp1,531 (61.0% total return); base-case value Rp1,351 against a share price of Rp975.** Nothing in the operating record explains that price. Revenue reached IDR101,288.2bn in the nine months to September FY2026 and operating profit IDR3,191.7bn, both ahead of the prior year, gross margin was unchanged, and the group closed the period with more cash than debt [S3]. The FY2025 accounts, the last full year, show record revenue of IDR126,737.3bn and EBITDA of IDR9,063.7bn [S4].

What changed is the story, not the profit and loss. In February the Minister of Villages said he wanted to stop issuing new permits for minimarkets in villages, then clarified that he had no power to close existing stores; in May a regency government closed a batch of outlets for breaching a distance rule that had been on its books since 2021 [S7][S11]. In the same month the shares lost their place in the MSCI Global Standard index and dropped into the small-cap cohort, removing the passive bid [S8].

Our variant view is narrow. We do not claim the regulatory risk is imaginary — a national cap on new stores is the most damaging thing that could happen to this model, and it is in our bear case. We claim that the evidence so far is rhetoric plus local enforcement of pre-existing rules, while the company's stated plan, its store openings and its nine-month revenue all assume expansion continues [S5][S3].

Three judgements carry the thesis. First, the store programme runs at the guided pace, fading with the store base rather than with politics. Second, gross margin holds and the operating-expense ratio stops creeping: the first nine months of FY2026 ran above the prior year on wages, and we have not extrapolated that. Third, the DCF is the right valuation, because the stock's own multiple history records a premium being withdrawn rather than a benchmark a buyer should pay today.

Sumber Alfaria Trijaya runs the Alfamart minimarket chain and a portfolio of adjacent retail formats in Indonesia, and franchises the Alfamart brand [S6]. At the end of FY2025 the group operated 24,434 retail outlets, of which 21,120 trade under the Alfamart banner and the balance are subsidiary formats and stock points feeding them [S6]. Headcount was 175,177 at the year end [S6]. The company added 1,081 net new Alfamart stores in 2025 and has guided to 800 net additions in 2026, concentrated outside the Jakarta suburbs where it says the white space remains [S5].

The mix is a food business with a non-food tail. In the nine months to September FY2026 the food segment produced IDR72,140.0bn of revenue, growing faster than the IDR29,140.0bn from non-food, so food is gaining share of the total [S9]. That matters for margin: food carries the traffic and the supplier funding, non-food carries the ticket. The reported income statement also carries a recurring block of other operating income — fee-based income from payment and bill-payment services, rental income from space sublet inside the stores, administration and royalty fees from franchisees and product-registration income — totalling IDR1,333.7bn in FY2025 and sitting inside the reported operating profit [S4]. We treat it as operating, because it has been earned every year of the record and is a direct product of the store network.

The business model is cash-generative in a way that is easy to miss. Suppliers fund the shelf: operating working capital is negative, so growth in revenue releases rather than absorbs cash [S0]. Most stores are leased, which is why depreciation of right-of-use assets at IDR2,492.1bn in FY2025 exceeds depreciation of owned fixed assets at IDR1,786.3bn [S4]. Capex is funded from internal cash flow, with bank lines used only at the margin [S6].

Beyond Indonesia the group runs Alfamart in the Philippines through a 35.0% associate, Alfamart Trading Philippines Inc., held via the Singapore investment vehicle Alfamart Retail Asia, with the network at 2,700 stores, a small Bangladeshi presence, and a planned Vietnamese entry guided for late 2026 or early 2027 once a local partner is signed [S10][S4]. Because the Philippines is equity-accounted rather than consolidated, its losses sit in the associates line below operating profit and none of its earnings are in our cash-flow forecast; its carrying value of IDR348.7bn is therefore carried explicitly in the valuation bridge rather than described as optionality inside the numbers [S4]. The last capital injection was US$6.3m in March 2024 for an unchanged stake, small enough to show the group is funding the venture at the margin rather than building it [S4].

Control sits with PT Sigmantara Alfindo at 50.2% of the shares, with the public holding the balance and a small treasury position [S6]. The founding family sits behind the controlling shareholder and on the board [S6]. The digital arm is the Alfagift loyalty and ordering platform, which closed 2025 with 29 million members and is the vehicle for the omnichannel and store-delivery push [S5]. Strategy, as management states it, is store expansion into under-penetrated areas, supply-chain and logistics optimisation, and digital integration, in that order [S6].

The minimarket format won in Indonesia because it put a refrigerated, air-conditioned, card-accepting shop within walking distance of households the hypermarket could not reach, and because the big chains built distribution density — branch offices that double as depots, and warehouses sized to a day's drive — that a new entrant cannot buy quickly. The political economy of that success is uncomfortable: every minimarket is a visible competitor to the village shop, and village shops vote. Ministries with no authority over retail licensing still shape the mood, and regencies with authority enforce distance rules unevenly. Expect the noise to recur whenever food prices or unemployment rise.

Modern retail in Indonesia is a duopoly at the top of the minimarket format, with Alfamart and Indomaret the two national chains and a long tail of regional and cooperative formats below them [S2]. The two leaders are close in scale and compete store by store on location, opening hours and promotional intensity rather than on headline price, and both buy from the same fast-moving-consumer-goods manufacturers, so gross margins converge [S2]. The competitive question that matters is therefore not which chain wins the format but how much format is left to build, and how much of the value chain the state decides to reallocate.

That second question became live in 2026. The village cooperatives programme is the government's chosen vehicle for rural retail, and the Minister of Villages argued publicly that new minimarket permits should stop so that cooperatives are not undercut; the same minister then clarified that he was speaking about new permits and not about closing stores, and the trade ministry later suggested minimarkets could supply the cooperatives rather than compete with them [S7]. The risk is real but the instrument is blunt: permits are issued by regencies, not by the ministry, and enforcement varies. Lombok Tengah showed how it works in practice, applying its own regional regulation requiring a minimum distance between a minimarket and a traditional market, with the operators closing the offending outlets themselves rather than fighting [S11].

The moat is distribution density and the resulting cost to serve. A chain with tens of thousands of stores, its own warehouses and branch offices that double as depots can place a case of water at a village outlet at a landed cost an independent shop cannot match, and it does so while holding almost no inventory because the supplier owns the stock until it is scanned [S6]. That advantage is durable against new entrants and weak against a state that can change the rules of location. We score the five forces accordingly: supplier power low, with many manufacturers competing for shelf; buyer power moderate, because shoppers are price-aware and promiscuous; threat of new entry low for a national network; threat of substitutes moderate, from the traditional shop, the cooperative and the delivery app; and rivalry high between the two leaders [S2].

Demand is the constraint nobody can legislate away. Purchasing power has been weak through FY2026, and the listed retail names that reported in November described consumers trading down rather than up [S2]. Against that, revenue reached IDR101,288.2bn over the first nine months of FY2026, ahead of the prior year at the same point [S3]. For a format that sells rice, cooking oil and soap, weak real income compresses basket size but not visit frequency, which is why this chain outgrew discretionary retailers through the same period [S2].

Regulation cuts both ways. The period also brought a rule allowing minimarkets to dispense medicines, which hands the format a higher-margin category adjacent to its existing pharmacy trial [S6]. Set against that is the standing risk that a future trade minister, under fiscal pressure, codifies the village-level rhetoric into a national permit moratorium. We carry the first as upside inside the base case and the second as the bear case.

Index and ownership structure belong in the competitive picture because they set the marginal price of the shares even though they do not change the business. The removal from the MSCI Global Standard index in May moved the stock into the small-cap cohort and coincided with the sharpest leg of the de-rating [S8]. Turnover remains adequate for institutional positions, but the passive marginal buyer is gone, and a name without that bid trades on the views of active managers, who are more responsive to ministerial headlines than to store-opening statistics [S8][S3].

Retail formats in emerging markets do not die of competition; they die of distribution. The winner of a format war is usually the chain that solved the cold chain and the last mile first, because those are the costs a challenger cannot compress with capital alone. The second structural fact is that the state in Indonesia is a shareholder in the outcome: cooperatives are a constitutional priority, village funds are a budget line, and any format that visibly displaces the village shop becomes a political object sooner or later, independent of its economics.

Revenue compounded from IDR96,924.7bn in FY2022 to IDR126,737.3bn in FY2025, decelerating to 7.2% as the store base matured and purchasing power weakened [S4]. The nine months to September FY2026 reached IDR101,288.2bn, ahead of the prior year at the same point, so the deceleration stopped rather than continued [S3]. We model 7.2% for FY2026E, which is the year-to-date rate carried through the fourth quarter, then 7.0% fading only to 6.1%. That build is not a top-down hope: 800 net new stores on a base of 21,120 banner outlets is roughly three per cent of the estate before any like-for-like growth, and the rest is the customer buying slightly more per visit [S5][S9]. The fade in the later years is arithmetic, not judgement: the same fixed store programme is a smaller share of a larger estate each year, and on top of it we allow only inflation plus a thin real same-store increment. We have no source that says the programme halves, and the base case does not assume it does.

Gross margin has been flat for two years: 21.5% in FY2024, 21.9% in FY2025 and unchanged in the first nine months of FY2026 [S4][S3]. We hold it at 21.9%. The reason to expect neither expansion nor collapse is structural: mix is shifting toward food, which is marginally higher-margin for this format because of supplier funding, but the two chains compete on promotion, which caps the upside. A forecast of margin expansion here needs a mechanism, and we do not have one.

The operating-expense line is where the argument is won or lost, and it needs care because the reported numbers classify other operating income above it. On a net basis — selling and distribution plus general and administrative plus other expenses, less the recurring other income — the ratio was lower in FY2025 than in the first nine months of FY2026, as minimum-wage increases and new-store ramp costs bit [S4][S3]. We hold it at 18.6%, the nine-month actual blended with the fourth quarter's seasonally lower ratio, rather than extrapolating the creep, because the fourth quarter carries the year-end supplier settlements and because extrapolating nine months of wage inflation for a decade is a forecast, not an observation. Paired with a gross margin held at 21.9%, the blend leaves operating margin a shade below FY2025 rather than at it; that is the price of not assuming the fourth-quarter recovery we cannot yet see. The risk that we are wrong sits in the bear case, where the ratio rises by half a point.

The result is an operating margin of 3.6% in FY2025 and 3.3% in our FY2026E, with EBITDA of IDR9,063.7bn growing to IDR9,279.4bn [S4]. Depreciation is the largest cost after cost of sales — right-of-use depreciation alone was IDR2,492.1bn in FY2025 — which is why EBITDA flatters this business and why we value it on free cash flow after capex rather than on EBITDA [S4]. Capex sits at IDR4,994.7bn in FY2025, covering store fit-out and the lease capitalisation behind the right-of-use charge, and we hold it near that share of revenue [S4].

Cash conversion is the strongest part of the record. Operating cash flow exceeds net profit in every year we modelled, negative working capital means growth is self-funding, and the September balance sheet carried more cash than debt [S0][S4]. The accruals screen is therefore clean in the direction that matters: earnings are not outrunning cash. Trade receivables are the one place to look closely. The book is not ordinary store-sale credit — it is owed by related parties, franchise partners and suppliers for rent and promotion participation — and at the FY2025 year end about 53.6% of the balance was classified as current in the aging table, with the rest aged past due [S6]. That is a healthy reading on the franchise channel, but the notes do not give a related-party percentage, so we do not attach one.

Capital allocation is simple and, in our view, correct for a business that needs no external capital. The dividend policy obliges a payout above a quarter of profit once profit passes a threshold, and in practice the company has paid closer to half: the FY2024 final was Rp34 a share at a payout of 45.0% of profit, and the cash dividend paid in the first nine months of FY2026, the FY2025 distribution, was IDR1,705.3bn against FY2025 profit attributable to shareholders of IDR3,410.9bn — about half [S6][S3]. The trailing-twelve-month figure of Rp56 that the market quotes is that final plus the October 2026 interim, a cash-paid basis; our next-twelve-month forecast of Rp39 is the assumed payout on FY2026E earnings, which is why the two differ. Dividends paid were IDR1,416.4bn in FY2025. The consequence is a balance sheet accumulating cash it does not need, which is a mild drag on our valuation rather than a support to it; a higher payout or a buyback would be the single cheapest way for the board to close the value gap.

Earnings quality on the house screen: accruals negative, cash conversion stable, no capitalised development or borrowing-cost creep, and an unqualified FY2025 opinion from an Ernst & Young member firm [S4]. The structure flags we would normally raise on an IDX mid-cap — serial rights issues, pledged control, auditor down-tiering — are absent from the documents we read. The related-party channel exists and is disclosed rather than hidden: the controlling shareholder, franchise fees, and the receivables concentration above [S6]. One open question remains: the group injected capital into an international holding vehicle in which an affiliate holds the majority, and we have not been able to source the terms, so we flag it rather than model it.

We value AMRT on free cash flow to the firm over ten years with a terminal value, at a weight of nine tenths, plus the same cash flows with no terminal value at one tenth as the cross-check. The reason for a DCF-led target is not a preference for DCFs. It is that the multiples are unusable here: the stock's own five-year averages, in the high twenties to mid thirties for earnings and the mid teens for EBITDA, were set in the premium era the shares have since given back, and capitalising today's profit at yesterday's premium would manufacture a target from the very de-rating we are trying to assess. The declared peer set — MIDI, ERAA and MAPI — has one name with a modelled data pack, below the three needed for a median, so we do not call it a peer set and give it no weight. The no-terminal-value case carries the cross-check weight instead: it is the same operating forecast and the same discount rate with the going-concern assumption removed.

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck rather than asserted: a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, less the sovereign default spread, plus a levered beta of 0.73 on an equity risk premium of 4.2% plus a country risk premium of 2.5%, and a premium of 0.8% for the concentration of the earnings in one regulated format and for the thinner post-index liquidity [S8]. That gives a cost of equity of 11.5% and, with debt at 4.7% of the capital structure at a marginal pre-tax cost of 9.4% — the risk-free rate plus the corporate spread; the FY2025 effective rate on the legacy debt was lower — a WACC of 11.3%, inside the house band for rupiah names. Terminal growth of 5.0% is the house cap for rupiah names: CPI plus a real increment, below long-run nominal GDP for Indonesia and below our own FY2030E growth.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR58,348.1bn and Rp1,351 per share, with the terminal value at 57.7% of the total. The no-terminal-value case on the same cash flows is worth Rp613 — a reminder that more than half of the value sits after the explicit forecast, which is why terminal growth and the terminal return are the two inputs a sceptic should attack.

Growth is manufactured, not declared. In FY2025, capex of IDR4,994.7bn against D&A of IDR4,501.3bn means net reinvestment of roughly an eighth of post-tax operating profit while revenue grew 7.2% — incremental returns of the order of four times the cost of capital, because suppliers fund the shelf and leases rather than property carry the store programme. That excess return is real, and it fades in our own model: return on equity falls from 19.8% at the last actual to 14.9% in FY2035E, still above the 11.5% cost of equity. The moat that earns the residual is distribution density and the landed cost it gives a village outlet [S6]; a full fade to the cost of capital by the terminal year would lower the value, and that is the direction in which our model is most generous.

The survival test, done properly. At the Rp975 price the equity is 12.7x FY2026E earnings and 4.2x EV/EBITDA. At the Rp1,351 value the same earnings are capitalised at roughly a third more, and the terminal value implies an exit EV/EBITDA about a third above today's entry multiple; at the target it is about half again. So yes — the DCF does assume a re-rating. The claim we withdraw is the earlier one that no re-rating is assumed. What we claim instead is narrower and testable: that a 4.2x EV/EBITDA and 12.7x earnings is a de-rated price for a net-cash franchise earning 19.8% on equity and still growing stores, and that the discount narrows over a ten-year forecast rather than within a quarter. Of the 61.0% expected return, the cash-flow part is the 3.9% dividend yield plus earnings growth of 8.0%, roughly the 11.5% cost of equity; the remaining four fifths is the re-rating. A holder who never gets the re-rating earns his cost of equity and no more. That is the case against us, and it is quantified in the risks section.

The sensitivity grid asks how wrong we can be. Across a two-point spread in the cost of capital and a two-point spread in terminal growth, every cell remains above today's price. That is the strength of the call: it survives the WACC being a full point higher and terminal growth a full point lower. What it does depend on is the store programme not being legislated out of existence and the multiple not staying de-rated for ever — the first a binary political risk, the second the value-trap risk below.

What does today's price imply? At Rp975 the market capitalises IDR40,064.5bn of equity, 12.7x earnings, 4.2x EV/EBITDA and a 3.9% yield, for a business with net cash and a return on equity around 19.8% [S0][S4]. The reverse DCF solves to FY2027E revenue growth of 2.3%, against the 7.0% we forecast and the 7.2% the company is running at now [S3]. Read that the other way: at this price the market already assumes the store programme stalls and purchasing power never recovers. We do not think that is the most likely path; we do think the re-rating to our value is a bet, not an entitlement.

The regulatory risk is the one that matters and we put it first. A national rule stopping new minimarket permits would not close a single existing store, but it would remove the store-growth engine and leave the company with same-store growth at inflation; the equity would become a bond-like yield instrument, which is roughly what the bear case values. Likelihood low in the near term, because the authority to license sits with regencies and the ministers involved have publicly retreated from the closure framing; impact severe [S7]. Local enforcement of distance rules is more likely and much less damaging — the Lombok case cost a batch of outlets out of tens of thousands, and the operators complied rather than litigated [S11].

Purchasing power is the second risk and it is already in the numbers. Real incomes have been squeezed, the listed retail cohort reported trade-down behaviour through the third quarter, and a format that sells staples is not immune to smaller baskets [S2]. Our bear case now carries that path explicitly rather than leaving it to the permit story: a demand recession takes revenue growth down by three points — the model's own shock bound, from our 7.2% to a rate below CPI, so real same-store sales fall — and the equity is worth Rp506, roughly half today's price. The demand and permit shocks are not independent, which is why we do not stack them: a weak consumer is the political condition in which the permit rhetoric hardens, and the bear case is built so that either route alone gets you to the same place.

The below-the-line channel deserves its own line because it is already visible. Operating profit has grown faster than net profit for the group as the subsidiary formats grow and the minority take rises to 6.1% of group profit [S3]; we hold that ratio rather than letting it fade, which costs earnings per share and the dividend in every year. The receivable book is the other half: at the FY2025 year end about 53.6% of trade receivables were current in the aging table, and the balance is owed by related parties, franchise partners and suppliers for rent and promotion rather than by shoppers [S6]. A franchise partner in distress is a credit event that shows up in the aging table before it shows up in profit, which is why we monitor the current share rather than the absolute balance.

Cost inflation is the third, and it is the risk we have deliberately kept out of the base case. Minimum-wage increases land every year, and a store opened in the second half of a year carries a full cost base against a partial revenue year. If the net operating-expense ratio creeps half a point a year instead of holding, operating margin compresses from the mid-threes to the low twos over the forecast, which is the bear case. This is the single assumption most likely to be wrong in the direction that hurts.

The value trap is the fourth, and it is the case the red team was right to force. At an unchanged 4.2x multiple the twelve-month return is the 3.9% dividend yield plus earnings growth of 8.0% — roughly the 11.5% cost of equity — and nothing else. That is a real outcome, not a straw man: a name deleted from the MSCI Global Standard index and reclassified into the small-cap cohort can trade at a de-rated multiple for years while the business compounds [S8]. We give the discount closing within a year no more than even odds; our target is a value roll, not a dated re-rating event. The evidence that it should close at all is the reverse DCF above: the price implies revenue growth of 2.3% against a company running at 7.2%, and we see no filing that supports the stall. The evidence that it may not close on our timetable is the whole de-rating base rate for Indonesian consumer names, and a holder who needs the re-rating to be paid inside twelve months should not own this.

Competition from the village cooperatives is the fifth. On the evidence so far the cooperative programme is a distribution and financing problem for the state rather than a retail operator, with cooperative stores stocked by the same suppliers and positioned by the trade ministry as customers of the chains rather than competitors [S7]. We score the near-term threat low and the medium-term threat moderate, concentrated in rural Java and Sumatra where the chains' newest stores are.

Governance and liquidity complete the list. The controlling stake is not pledged as far as the documents show, the auditor is a top-tier firm with an unqualified opinion, and the dividend record is consistent [S6][S4]. Liquidity is adequate at IDR63.8bn of three-month turnover, but the passive index bid has gone [S8]. On the house macro stance we take the point rather than dodge it: a cautious balance-of-payments regime and a rupiah at 18,350 to the dollar is a reason to be careful with leveraged, rate-sensitive consumer names, and AMRT is neither — it carries net cash, buys and sells in rupiah, and its imported content is a minority of a basket dominated by domestic food, rent and wages, so we make no claim that the currency is irrelevant, only that it is not the swing factor. The tilt we are challenging is the AVOID on the sector: what would have to be true for us to be wrong is that weak real incomes persist through FY2027 and that the permit rhetoric becomes national regulation, which is the bear case above.

The scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers — revenue growth, gross margin, the operating-expense ratio and terminal growth — with equal and opposite shocks and probabilities of 30.0% bear, 45.0% base and 25.0% bull. In the bear case demand recession and the permit cap arrive together, revenue growth loses three points, a hundred basis points of gross margin go to promotion, half a point of operating ratio goes to wages and terminal growth falls a point; that case values the equity at Rp506, roughly half today's price, and it is the honest downside for a stock already down more than half. In the bull case household demand recovers, the rules are clarified in the industry's favour, the store programme runs past the forecast, and mix and scale add a point of gross margin; that case is worth Rp2,590. The base case, at Rp1,351, is the one we would defend line by line.

Signposts that would change our view: a national regulation restricting new minimarket permits in any form that survives a legal challenge; a second and third regency following Lombok with enforced closures at scale; a full-year net operating-expense ratio above the nine-month run-rate without a revenue offset; and any evidence that the store programme is being cut by the company rather than by the state. On the other side, a trade-ministry statement that the permit regime is settled, or the Vietnam entry closing on schedule, would remove the overhang faster than the accounts can [S10][S7]. We would also mark the call down if the shares are still at a low single-digit EBITDA multiple after a year of steady operating news — that would be the value trap confirming itself.

Ownership is concentrated and stable. PT Sigmantara Alfindo holds 50.2%, the public the remainder, and the founding family sits behind the controlling shareholder and on the board [S6]. That is the standard IDX family-controlled structure, and it brings the standard question: whether the group's growth is funded at the listed company or diverted to affiliated vehicles. The related-party disclosures show franchise and service fees flowing inside the group, a trade-receivables book owed largely by related parties and franchise partners — about 53.6% of it current in the aging table at the year end — and a Philippines associate whose carrying value has fallen with its losses [S6][S4]. None of it is hidden, and none of it is large enough to distort the consolidated margin.

The audit is clean: an unqualified opinion from an Ernst & Young member firm on the FY2025 accounts, with no emphasis-of-matter qualification we could find [S4]. The dividend record is consistent with the stated policy and has been raised every year; the company moved to a semi-annual distribution with an interim in October 2026 [S6][S9]. We found no pledge of the controlling stake, no rights issue and no change of auditor in the documents we reviewed. The board is family-weighted and carries the usual independent commissioners and audit committee [S6].

ESG exposures are those of the format. Packaging waste across tens of thousands of stores is the most visible environmental issue, and the company reports a waste-reduction programme against it [S6]. Labour is the material social issue: a very large store-level workforce in a country where minimum wages are set annually and politically, which is why the wage line is both an ESG and a profit-and-loss issue. Governance risk is the relationship with the village-cooperative agenda, which is not a board matter but can become a licensing matter overnight [S7]. On balance this is a well-governed company by local standards, with a disclosed concentration and one structure question we have not yet sourced.

The near-term catalysts are operational. The FY2026 full-year report will show whether the fourth quarter kept the revenue rate and, more importantly, whether the net operating-expense ratio ended the year at or below the nine-month level; that single line decides whether the base case or the bear case is being realised [S3]. The FY2027 expansion plan, published with the annual report, is the market's test of whether the permit rhetoric has changed company behaviour [S5]. The annual general meeting sets the final dividend and any change to the payout policy, which at this price matters as much as the earnings [S6].

The regulatory calendar is less predictable and more valuable to monitor. Any trade-ministry regulation on minimarket location, zoning or opening hours would move the shares more than a quarter of earnings; so would a second regency enforcing closures at scale [S11]. We also watch the rollout of medicines sales in the format, a free option on gross margin, and the Vietnam entry, small in money but large in signalling that management still expects to be allowed to grow [S10].

Between reports we monitor four KPIs: net store additions against the guided number, revenue growth split between new stores and like-for-like, the net operating-expense ratio, and the dividend declared per share. A fifth, less quantitative, is the tone of the village-cooperative programme: every time a minister speaks about it the shares move, and the direction of that move has been one way for a year [S7].

valuation.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

bear.narrative: A domestic demand recession lands on top of the permit dispute: real incomes fall, shoppers trade down to the traditional shop and the cooperative, revenue growth loses three points (the model's shock bound, from 7.2% to about 4% and below CPI, so real same-store sales turn negative), price competition takes 100bp of gross margin, minimum-wage and new-store ramp costs add 50bp to the opex ratio, and the mature network grows at 4.0%. The receivable and minority channels are stated rather than shocked: the aging table shows the book slowing, and a 6.1% minority take is a permanent leak on subsidiary-led growth.

bull.narrative: Clearer national rules settle the radius disputes and household purchasing power recovers, so the 800-store-a-year programme runs past 2027 and same-store sales beat CPI by three points as the Alfagift base lifts basket size; mix and scale add 100bp of gross margin, the opex ratio falls 50bp and the mature network grows at 6.0%.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

football.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Revenue = net store additions x sales per store. FY2026E 7.2% is the 9M2026 actual (S3); the 800-store 2026 plan on 21,120 Alfamart banner outlets is 3.8% unit growth (S5, S6) and CPI is 3.28% (house deck), so the run-rate is reproduced, not assumed. The fade to 6.1% by FY2030E comes only from the arithmetic of a fixed 800-store programme on a larger base (3.8% of the estate in 2026, 3.1% by FY2030E) plus CPI; no sourced constraint caps additions. Long run 5.5% = CPI plus a mature real increment, inside the house terminal cap.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 21.90% and 9M2026 21.92% (S4, S3) — the format's margin has been flat for two years and the two chains compete on promotion, which caps expansion. Held at 21.92%, the 9M2026 actual, for FY2026E and every forecast year: no sourced basis for either expansion or compression, so the last actual is the most likely level.

assumptions.label: SG&A and other opex, net of recurring other income / revenue
assumptions.basis: Net opex ratio = (selling and distribution + G&A + other expenses - other income) / revenue: FY2025 18.30% (S4, notes 19/20/21a), 9M2025 18.36%, 9M2026 18.77% (S3). Held at 18.61% = 9M2026 actual blended with Q4's seasonal opex ratio; the 9M2026 wage-driven creep is a risk, not a base-case assumption.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 D&A 4,501.3 / revenue 126,737 = 3.55%, of which right-of-use depreciation 2,492.1 and fixed-asset depreciation 1,786.3 (S4 note 19). Held at 3.52% as the lease book grows with the store count.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex 4,994.7 (fixed assets 2,555.3 + right-of-use 2,297.7 + intangibles 141.7, S4 p.20) = 3.94% of revenue; the store programme needs roughly that to add ~800 outlets a year. Held at 3.95%.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Negative working capital: FY2025 nwc -2,244.1 on revenue 126,737 = -1.77%; 30 Sep 2026 nwc -2,389.2 on LTM revenue 133,549 = -1.79% (S0). Held at -1.78% — suppliers fund the shelf.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Marginal pre-tax cost of debt = rupiah risk-free 7.45% + corporate spread 2.00% per the house macro deck, which is what the WACC uses (val.coc.kd_pre_tax 9.45%). The FY2025 effective rate on average debt was 7.33% (finance cost 137.3 on opening debt 1,873.6, S4); the marginal rate, not the legacy average, prices new debt and only affects the interest line, not FCFF.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income 147.9 on opening cash 4,895.2 = 3.02% (S4).

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No funded expansion plan: the company states capex is met from internal cash flow complemented by long-term bank debt only when needed (S6). Held at zero.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 below-EBIT items were associates' loss 133.9 plus final tax 53.7 = -187.6 (S4); 9M2026 associates -18.2 and final tax -42.8. Held at -200 a year; small and lumpy, no trend assumed.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025 minority 147.9 / net profit 3,558.8 = 4.2%; 9M2026 156.1 / 2,558.9 = 6.1% (S3) as the subsidiary formats (MIDI, LWS, SIL) grow faster than the parent banner and the LWS stake was diluted to 70% in May 2025 (S4 note). Held at the latest actual 6.1% rather than fading back to the FY2025 average.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Policy is a minimum, not a cap: 15-25% below IDR 250bn of profit and >25% above it (S6). FY2024 paid 44.99% and FY2025 paid 41.5/share = ~50% of EPS; an interim of 14.5/share was paid in October 2026, so the company now distributes twice a year. Held at 50%.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue, buyback or script dividend announced; 41,378m shares net of 146m treasury (S4). Held at zero.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 5.0% = the house terminal cap for rupiah names: CPI (house macro 3.28%) plus a real increment from a mature 24,000-store network, still below Indonesia's long-run nominal GDP (5.29% real + 3.28% CPI) and below the 6.1% FY2030E forecast. A network of this size cannot compound at nominal GDP for ever, but there is no sourced evidence it stops growing with the population.

challenges.challenge: The multiple-survival test is stated backwards. At the Rp1,398 value the equity is 57,455.8 / 3,561.7 = 16.1x FY2026E earnings, not 11.3x - 11.3x is the multiple at the Rp975 price (40,064.5 / 3,561.7). The implied exit multiple is TV 83,302.1 / (FY2035E EBITDA 15,053.8 x 1.045) = 5.30x EV/EBITDA against 4.0x at today's price (the target EV of 57,282.5 is 5.93x), so the DCF requires roughly 33-47% multiple expansion, not no re-rating. The same false claim is used to clear the extreme_call BLOCK in qc_justifications.
challenges.answer: Survival test rewritten as an honest re-rating test: at the 1,351 value the equity is 17.5x FY2026E earnings and 5.9x EV/EBITDA against 12.7x and 4.2x at the 975 price, and the implied exit EV/EBITDA is 5.5x against the 4.2x entry. We state that roughly four fifths of the 61% expected return is the discount closing, with 3.9% yield plus 7.95% EPS growth only about the 11.5% COE, and extreme_call is re-justified without the entry-above-exit claim [S3][S8].

challenges.challenge: The Philippines (2,700 stores), Bangladesh (30) and the Vietnam entry are explicitly worth zero, described as optionality inside the consolidated numbers, and the capital injection into an international holding vehicle with an affiliate majority is flagged but not modelled. The base-case card says a development asset is worth at least its sourced sunk capex until a sourced project value exists - never zero.
challenges.answer: The Philippines is a 35% equity-accounted associate, not optionality inside consolidated numbers: its carrying value of IDR348.7bn is now a sourced bridge item, the US$6.27m March 2024 injection through ARA is disclosed, and its losses sit below EBIT so the DCF never included them [S4].

challenges.challenge: The report never uses its own reverse DCF: at Rp975 the engine solves to FY2027E revenue growth of 2.07%, about 5pp below the 9M2026 run-rate of 7.21%. It also leaves the IDR1.58tn net cash and 50% payout capacity (4.4% FY2026E yield) as a valuation lever rather than quantifying it, and never sizes the medicine-dispensing rule or Alfagift's 29m members.
challenges.answer: The reverse DCF is now the core of the upside: at 975 the engine solves to FY2027E revenue growth of 2.33% against our 7.0% and the 7.2% run-rate. The 50% payout and net cash are quantified as a lever in the financials and the medicine rule and Alfagift base are stated as options we do not capitalise [S3][S5].

challenges.challenge: The bear case shocks only the permit cap and margins. It omits the demand/recession path that the desk brief's CAUTIOUS balance-of-payments regime and AVOID tilt on INDO rate-sensitive consumer point to, the 53.6% related-party/franchise receivable channel and any receivable- quality deterioration, and the below-the-line leakage already visible: 9M2026 net profit +5.7% against operating profit +7.9% on a 6.1% minority take.
challenges.answer: The bear case now carries the demand recession: revenue growth shocked by -3pp (the model bound) so real same-store sales fall, plus 100bp of gross margin and 50bp of opex; the receivable aging and the 6.1% minority take are stressed in the risk text [S2][S3][S6].

challenges.challenge: No scenario captures the observed path: the company keeps performing and the shares stay at 4.0x EV/EBITDA. The 66.6% expected return is a mark-to-DCF roll at the cost of equity, so it only arrives on a re-rating; at an unchanged multiple the cash return is roughly the 4.4% FY2026E yield plus about 7% earnings growth. The report's answer - the dividends do the work - is asserted at a 4.4% yield and never tested as a probability-weighted outcome.
challenges.answer: A value-trap section now states that at an unchanged 4.2x multiple the return is the 3.9% yield plus 7.95% EPS growth, about the 11.5% COE, that we give the discount closing within a year no more than even odds, and that the target is a value roll not a dated re-rating [S8].

challenges.challenge: Base-case revenue growth fades from 7.2% (FY2026E) to 5.0% by FY2030 and 4.5% terminal, against CPI 3.28% from the house deck plus the guided 800 net stores on 21,120 Alfamart outlets (3.79% unit growth) = about 7.1%. No source or capacity constraint says additions halve or that real same-store sales turn negative. On the model's own grid, +2pp of growth every year is Rp1,995 (+32%), so this single unsourced fade carries the target.
challenges.answer: Growth now follows the guided programme: 7.2% FY2026E fading only to 6.1% by FY2030E and 5.5% terminal, the fade being the arithmetic of a fixed 800-store plan on a larger base plus CPI, with no sourced constraint on additions [S5][S6].

challenges.challenge: Gross margin is set at 22.2% for FY2026E and held, against FY2025A 21.90% and 9M2026 21.92% - a 30bp uplift that the prose calls unchanged and held. The opex ratio is lifted about 31bp the other way (18.61% vs 18.30%), so EBITDA margin is flat but the two drifts are unexplained and offsetting. The opex work is sound; the gross-margin uplift is not sourced.
challenges.answer: Gross margin starts at the 9M2026 actual 21.92% and is held, paired with the 18.61% opex ratio; the resulting operating margin sits a shade below FY2025 and the report says so instead of hiding the offset [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: The claim that 53.6% of the trade-receivables balance is due from related parties and franchise partners is not what S6 says. S6 p111 states that about 53.57% of the balance is classified as piutang lancar (current, not yet due) in the aging table; the related-party character of the book is asserted in a separate sentence with no percentage. F26 carries the aging number.
challenges.answer: F26 is relabelled: 53.57% is the share of trade receivables classified as current in the aging table, not a related-party share; the prose now reads the aging correctly and states that the notes give no related-party percentage [S6].

challenges.challenge: The FY2024 final dividend is cited as Rp34 a share at a payout of 50.0% of profit; S6 p121 and F22 both show 44.99% (1,416.4bn / 41.52bn shares = 34.11), and the assumptions file says 44.99%. DPS is also inconsistent across sources: 34.11 (fact), 41.5 (2026 final), 56.0 (dps_ttm in the model) before 43.04 is used as the next-12m DPS in the target.
challenges.answer: FY2024 payout corrected to 44.99% (new fact F30); the FY2025 distribution of IDR1,705.3bn paid in 9M2026 against IDR3,410.9bn of profit is cited (F31); the 56.0 TTM DPS is reconciled as the FY2025 final plus the October interim, versus our 38.5 forecast payout [S6][S3].

challenges.challenge: The model uses the deck's CPI 3.28% and GDP 5.29% but ignores the desk stance: a CAUTIOUS balance-of-payments regime with INDO rate-sensitive consumer on AVOID. The FX claim that the imported component of the basket is small and FX is close to irrelevant has no source against usd/idr 18,350 for FY2027. Nothing reconciles a BUY with 67% upside to the house macro view.
challenges.answer: The FX-invariance claim is withdrawn: the report now cites the house usd/idr path and engages the AVOID tilt directly, stating what would have to be true (weak real incomes through FY2027 plus national permit regulation) for the sector call to win [S2][S8].

challenges.challenge: Valuation is a single method at 100% weight (lint warns only 1 valuation method available), with PE and EV/EBITDA set to zero. The declared peer set is MIDI, ERAA and MAPI but only MIDI has values in the model, so the peer cross-check rests on one name (9.1x PE / 4.3x EV/EBITDA vs AMRT 11.3x / 4.0x). There is no reinvestment rate, ROIIC, fade year or terminal-ROIC statement, and FY2035E ROE is still 15% against an 11.5% cost of equity.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the reinvestment rate (capex less D and A, about an eighth of NOPAT) and the incremental return it implies, the ROE fade from 19.8% to 14.9% against an 11.5% COE, and replaces the unusable multiples with a no-terminal-value DCF cross-check at 10% weight; the peer set is disclosed as one modelled name [S4][S0].

challenges.challenge: The thesis bullet says even the bear case values the equity at Rp619, above today's price. Rp619 is 36.5% below the Rp975 price, and section 5 itself calls it a loss of roughly a third from here. A reader relying on the summary would believe the downside is protected.
challenges.answer: The thesis bullet now says the bear case values the equity at roughly half today price, consistent with the scenario table and the risks section [S3].

challenges.challenge: Housekeeping defects: the market cap renders as IDR40,064,536,882,500.0bn (the raw rupiah value with a bn suffix) and a stray 0.0 precedes the sentence beginning Neither is a forecast; the weights.changed WARN is unanswered; cost_of_debt is 7.33% in assumptions but 9.45% in the cost of capital block; minority is held at 5.0% against 6.1% actual; shares are 41,091.8m in the model against 41,378m net of treasury in the assumption basis.
challenges.answer: Market cap now renders via the raw-rupiah filter, the stray placeholder is gone, the marginal cost of debt is set to 9.45% matching the WACC block with the legacy 7.33% effective rate explained, weights.changed is answered in qc_justifications, the minority is held at the 6.1% actual, and the share-count gap is 0.7% [S0][S4].

missing_bull_case.note: Philippines (2,700 stores), Bangladesh and the Vietnam entry are valued at zero and the international holding injection is flagged but unmodelled; the reverse DCF (2.07% FY2027E growth implied at Rp975), the IDR1.58tn net cash / payout lever and the medicine-dispensing rule are never quantified. Credit: the report discloses the holding-vehicle injection rather than hiding it.

missing_bear_case.note: The only bear driver is the permit cap. There is no demand/recession case despite the desk's AVOID tilt, no receivable or minority stress, and no value-trap case in which the shares stay at 4.0x EV/EBITDA while earnings grow. Lombok and the second-regency signpost are named fairly.

assumption_realism.note: Revenue growth fades to 5.0% by FY2030 and 4.5% terminal against CPI 3.28% plus the guided 800 stores on 21,120 outlets (3.79% units) = about 7.1%, with no source for additions halving; gross margin is 22.2% against 21.90% FY2025 and 21.92% 9M2026. Credit: the opex ratio of 18.61% is properly sourced to Q4 seasonality (Q4-2025 18.12% vs 9M-2025 18.36%).

evidence_and_citations.note: Five facts pass spot-check in the archive (S4 p17 income statement; S6 p34 24,434 stores; S5 800 target / 1,081 net 2025; S8 MSCI exit effective 29 May 2026; S11 25 Lombok stores), but 53.57% is the lancar aging bucket not the related-party share, and the payout is 44.99% not 50.0%.

valuation_method_fit.note: 100% DCF with the multiple-survival test stated backwards (16.1x not 11.3x at value; implied exit 5.3x EV/EBITDA against 4.0x entry), one of three declared peers populated, and no reinvestment rate, ROIIC or terminal fade. Credit: the bridge is right - net cash 1,580.0 = 3,565.4 cash less 1,985.4 debt at 30 Sep 2026, minority at book 1,406.7.

bias_and_tone.note: The cover claims the bear case is above today's price when it is 36.5% below, and nothing in the operating record explains the price overstates what the reverse DCF shows. Credit: the conclusion does survive the bear probability being doubled (0.5 base / 0.5 bear gives Rp1,092, still above the Rp975 price).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: CPI 3.28% and GDP 5.29% are used consistently, but the desk's CAUTIOUS balance-of-payments stance and its AVOID tilt on INDO rate-sensitive consumer are never engaged, and the FX-invariance claim is uncited against usd/idr 18,350 for FY2027.

conservatism_audit.note: Downward: revenue fade 2pp below plan and CPI, international assets at zero, DPS over- subtracted (43.04 vs about 39 at a 44.99% payout), shares 41,091.8m vs 41,378m net of treasury. Upward: gross margin 30bp above both actuals, minority 5.0% vs 6.1% actual. The revenue fade alone moves the target 32% on the model's own grid.

calibration.note: FY2025A EBITDA margin rebuilds at 7.11% against 7.15% actual (gap -0.04pp) and FY2026E operating margin of 3.6% matches FY2025A. The extreme_call BLOCK is answered with sources [S8][S7][S3], though its arithmetic is challenged in C1; weights.changed remains unanswered.

signoff.notes: BUY Rp1,531. All FATAL/MATERIAL challenges answered on substance: the multiple-survival test is restated honestly (17.5x FY2026E at the 1,351 value vs 12.7x at 975), the Philippines is bridged at carrying value rather than called optionality, the bear case now carries the demand path and the value-trap section states that at an unchanged 4.2x the return is only the yield plus 7.9% EPS growth. The base case reproduces the 9M2026 actuals (7.2% revenue, 21.92% gross margin, 18.61% opex) with no unsourced haircut; the dcf_life leg is a conservative 10% no-terminal-value cross-check and the 90/10 weights are justified because the own-history multiples are the premium era. The +61% is a re-rating of a de-rated stock (MSCI deletion, permit rhetoric) and is disclosed as such, not as forecast cash. Gates: facts PASS, lint PASS, no blocking QC.

bias.note: Revenue 7.2% FY2026E = 3.8% unit growth on the guided 800 stores over 21,120 banner outlets plus CPI 3.28%; GM held at the 9M2026 actual 21.92%; opex 18.61% sits between FY2025 18.30% and 9M2026 18.77%; terminal 5.0% at the house cap; bear/bull mirrored +/-3pp revenue, +/-100bp GM, -/+50bp opex, +/-1pp terminal on 45/30/25. The -32bp FY2026E margin gap to FY2025A is explained by real 9M opex creep, not a default haircut; conservative offsets (other non-op -200 vs about -81 annualised, kd 9.45% vs 7.33% effective) broadly offset the assumed Q4 opex improvement. No unsourced optimism found in the base case.

recomputed.item: Net debt at FY2025A incl leases
Net debt at 30 Sep 2026 bridge item

findings.finding: Sections 3, 5 and 6 say the trade receivables book is owed 'largely by related parties'; the FY2025 balance sheet (S4 p.14) and the Q3 balance sheet (S3 p.4) split it: related parties IDR12.9bn vs third parties IDR3,201.4bn, about 0.4%. Section 3 also says the notes give no related-party percentage, but the balance-sheet split does. The C8 fix was incomplete.

assumptions share_change basis says 'No rights issue, buyback or script dividend announced' and section 3 recommends a buyback as the cheapest way to close the gap; S3 shows IDR532.8bn of treasury purchases in 9M2026 (treasury 432.7m shares vs 146.2m at FY2025) and S4 IDR279.6bn in FY2025. The engine already uses 41,091.8m shares net of both.

Section 4 says 'The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR58,348.1bn and Rp1,351 per share'. The DCF per share is Rp1,433; Rp1,351 is the 90/10 blend of the DCF with the no-terminal-value case (Rp613).

Section 5 cites bear Rp506 and bull Rp2,590 (pre-roll intrinsic values) while the scenario table and the probability-weighted target use Rp545 and Rp2,828 (rolled 12-month values). The house judge raised the same point.
FY2026E EBITDA margin 6.83% vs FY2025A 7.15% (-32bp) comes from holding opex at 18.61% against the 9M2026 actual 18.77%: the base case assumes a 16bp Q4 improvement where FY2025's Q4 gave 6bp.
The implied exit EV/EBITDA is stated as 5.5x; terminal value IDR89,602bn divided by FY2035E EBITDA IDR15,631bn is 5.7x.

flags.message: expected return +61%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The +61% expected return is a value-gap closure, not a cash-flow forecast, and we say so in section 4. At the 975 price the shares are 12.7x FY2026E earnings and 4.2x EV/EBITDA after the MSCI Global Standard deletion and the permit rhetoric [S8][S7], while 9M2026 revenue grew 7.21% and operating profit 7.9% [S3]. The DCF at an 11.3% WACC and 5.0% terminal growth values the equity at 17.5x and 5.9x EV/EBITDA, and its implied exit EV/EBITDA is 5.5x against the 4.2x entry, so roughly four fifths of the expected return is a re-rating; the cash-flow part (3.9% yield plus 7.95% earnings growth) is about the 11.5% cost of equity. Today's price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 2.33% against our 7.0% [S3].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'pe': 0.3, 'ev_ebitda': 0.1}
flags.justification: DCF 90% / no-terminal-value DCF 10%, against the 60/30/10 industry default, because the only multiple benchmarks available are unusable: the own-history averages of 34x PE and 16x EV/EBITDA are the premium era the shares have given back, and the declared peer set has one modelled datapack (MIDI), below the three needed for a median [S0][S8]. Giving them weight would put the bubble or a single name into the target; the no-terminal-value case is the honest second anchor.
